passage:
Day 1. At the Monday meeting, Vasudha, frustrated by three bugs, put the code on the big screen. "Vinita, line 42 again. Did you even run it?" Nobody laughed. Vinita's ears went red.

Day 8. In stand-up Vinita said only "fine" and asked no questions, though the comments on her ticket showed she was stuck.

Day 20. A customer reported a crash in a module Vinita had touched. The history showed a problem Vinita had noticed a week earlier and never mentioned. Two more bugs turned up in the same module that afternoon.

qa.q: Which line did Vasudha point out on the big screen?
How did Vinita feel when the code was shown to the whole team?
qa.a: Vinita felt embarrassed and humiliated, as her ears going red suggests.

qa.q: What could Vasudha have done instead, and why?
qa.a: Vasudha could have spoken to Vinita privately about the bugs and asked what would help, because criticism in private keeps questions and honesty alive.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team have been affected?
qa.a: The rest of the team probably felt uneasy, worried they might be next, and less willing to admit their own mistakes.

grounding: Illustrates a frustrated lead pointing out mistakes in front of the team so the junior withdraws, stops asking questions and hides errors.

passage:
Siddharth, you asked why I'm so careful when I correct people. Let me, Dolma, tell you about my worst year as a lead, at the travel agency in Gangtok.
We had a new junior, Pemba, who kept booking the wrong dates. One morning, in front of all eight of us, I held up his booking sheet and said, "How can anyone make this mistake three times?" I thought shame would make him careful.
It did the opposite. He stopped asking me anything. When he wasn't sure about a date, he just guessed and kept quiet. When a customer complained, he'd already hidden the email.
Two months later, a family arrived at the airport with no hotel. Pemba had known about the error for a week.
That's when I understood. My loud voice didn't fix his mistakes. It only taught him to hide them.

qa.q: How many people were there when Dolma held up the booking sheet?
How did Pemba feel after being criticised in front of everyone, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Pemba felt humiliated and afraid; he stopped asking questions, guessed quietly and hid a customer complaint.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Dolma's story, and what could Dolma have chosen instead that morning?
qa.a: The turning point was the public criticism; Dolma could have spoken to Pemba privately with the three examples and asked what was making the dates hard.

qa.q: How did the public criticism affect the family who arrived at the airport?
qa.a: The family was left with no hotel, because Pemba had hidden the error for a week instead of asking for help.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how criticising a junior's mistakes in front of the team made him withdraw, stop asking and hide errors, so the problem grew.

passage:
The audit was at nine the next morning, the office generator had failed, and Nitin was reading Simran's reconciliation sheets by the light of a phone torch.
He found a wrong total on page three. He had already found two that afternoon.
"Simran," he said loudly, so the whole team, huddled around the one working laptop, heard. "Three errors in one file. Did you even check this before sending it?"
Simran's face went red. "I'm sorry, I'll fix it."
"Everyone, look. This is what happens when people rush."
Nobody said anything. After that night, Simran stopped asking Nitin questions. She sent files without comments. When she spotted a mistake of her own a week later, she corrected it quietly and didn't mention it.
A month on, the auditors found four errors that nobody had caught. Two were Simran's, hidden in files she had been afraid to flag.

qa.q: How many errors did Nitin say were in the file?
What was Simran feeling when her face went red?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and ashamed at being criticised in front of the whole team.

qa.q: What would you change first in Nitin's approach, even under the audit pressure?
qa.a: Point out the errors to Simran privately and ask what made the file hard, so she keeps flagging problems instead of hiding them.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team see Nitin's outburst?
qa.a: They may feel uneasy and wary, learning that mistakes get public shame, which makes everyone less likely to admit errors.

grounding: It shows a frustrated lead criticising a junior's mistakes in front of the team, after which the junior stops asking questions and hides errors.
